meta.title: Cutting CI pipeline time by 40% | Pedro Morago
meta.description: How I balanced end-to-end tests across parallel CI containers at IriusRisk with a MILP model in Python, and cut pipeline time by 40% with no extra infrastructure.
meta.shareDescription: At IriusRisk, end-to-end tests were split unevenly across parallel CI containers. An optimization model I built fixed the split and cut pipeline time by 40%.

title: Cutting CI pipeline time by 40%
lede: At IriusRisk, our end-to-end tests ran in parallel CI containers split by product module, and the largest module held up every pipeline. I stated the split as an optimization problem, weighed time against cost, and cut pipeline time by 40% at the same cost.

facts.label: Company
facts.text: IriusRisk, an international cybersecurity SaaS for threat modeling

facts.label: My role
facts.text: QA Engineer. I designed the model and deployed it.

facts.label: Tools
facts.text: Python, PuLP and the CBC solver

facts.label: Result
facts.text: 40% less pipeline time at the same cost, measured on real runs after deployment

blocks.text: Our end-to-end test files, or specs, ran in parallel CI containers, one container per product module. Modules are not the same size, so neither were the containers. The container of the largest module ran for more than twice as long as the shortest one, and a pipeline is only done when its slowest container is.

Every container also spent the same fixed time on setup before its first spec ran, close to half of a balanced container's run. So adding containers was not free: each new one paid the full setup again, and we paid for every minute each container ran.
In maths you state a problem precisely before you try to solve it. This is the pipeline problem, stated that way.

rows.label: Given
rows.text: The end-to-end specs, each with its average duration from real runs, the fixed setup time of a container, and the cost of a container per minute.

rows.label: Rules
rows.text: Every spec runs in exactly one container. A container is done when its setup and all its specs are done. The pipeline is done when its last container is.

rows.label: Goals
rows.text: A short pipeline and a low cost. More containers make the pipeline shorter but cost more, so the two goals pull against each other.

blocks.text: Two goals that pull against each other make it a multi-criteria optimization problem. There is no single best answer, only a set of best trade-offs, and the job is to find that set and then choose from it.

A model is only as good as its numbers, so I started from the CI logs of real runs: every module, both the sanity and the regression suites, over several CI cycles. With Python I parsed each log and worked out the average duration of every spec, and the setup time of every container.

Failing tests needed care. A test that fails and is retried adds time that says nothing about how long the spec normally takes. So I separated them, measured how much time each CI cycle lost to failures and retries, and kept two data sets: the pipeline as it really ran, and the same pipeline without those failures.

Then I used PuLP, a Python library for optimization, to build a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model. For each spec and each container there is a yes-or-no variable: does this container run this spec? The constraints say that every spec runs exactly once and that no container, setup included, runs longer than the pipeline time. The model makes that time as short as possible.

It's like loading parcels of different sizes into vans so that the last van to finish its round finishes as early as possible. The CBC solver found splits that are provably optimal, or within a fraction of a second of a lower bound I derived for the pipeline time.

With the model working, I solved it for every number of containers from 3 to 14. Each answer is a point on the Pareto frontier: the fastest pipeline you can get for that cost. The frontier made the trade-off visible. Doubling the containers cut the pipeline time by only about a quarter and raised the cost by almost half, because every extra container pays the full setup again.

To choose a point on the frontier, I used goal programming: set a target for time and a target for cost, weight them, and find the configuration that misses them by the least. I ran it for four scenarios.

items: Keep the current cost: the same number of containers we already had came out best.
Contain the cost: fewer containers, a cheaper run and a clearly longer pipeline.
Put time first: more containers, a faster pipeline and a higher bill.
A slower setup than measured: the choice held, so a bad day in CI would not change it.

blocks.text: The answer was not to buy more containers. It was to keep the ones we had and split the specs well.

I deployed the new split with the same number of containers and measured it on real runs. Pipeline time fell by 40% and the cost stayed the same. The measured time was within about 1% of what the model had predicted, which told me the data and the model described the pipeline well.

The data without failing tests gave one more result: fixing the tests that failed and were retried would cut the pipeline by roughly another tenth. That turned a vague feeling about flaky tests into a number the team could weigh against other work.

The split is only as good as the averages behind it. When specs are added or their durations change, the split has to be recomputed from fresh data. CI Shard Advisor, below, does that from new run reports each time.

Later I turned the idea into CI Shard Advisor, a public tool for Cypress suites. It reads your run reports and shows how evenly your containers finish. Then it recommends the split in which the slowest container finishes earliest, as a list of specs for each container that you can paste into GitHub Actions or Bitbucket Pipelines. It searches with branch and bound, an exact method that can prove no better split exists for the durations in your reports.

items: It opens in the browser with a demo run loaded. You can drop in your own reports, and they never leave the browser. There's nothing to install and no account to create.
It also runs as a command-line tool with a quality-gate mode, and as a local REST API.

blocks.text: How it's tested
All the optimization logic sits in a pure core with a hexagonal architecture, so it can be tested separately from the web app, the command-line tool and the API.

An optimizer is hard to test with fixed examples, because for most inputs nobody knows the right answer in advance. For small inputs you can find it by trying every possible split. So property-based tests generate hundreds of random small cases and check that branch and bound finds the same answer as that brute-force search, and that whenever it claims a split is optimal, it really is, even when the search is cut short. Metamorphic and invariant tests check other rules that any correct answer has to follow.
The local API also has its own Java suite in REST Assured and JUnit 5, including a check of the response against a JSON Schema.
Tech: TypeScript, React, Vite, Fastify, Node.js, pnpm, Playwright and k6.
Check whether the ones you already have finish at about the same time. If they don't, fixing the split may be cheaper than adding more.
